text:
In a database, a missing value is null. Not zero, not an empty string... no value at all. So for every column, ask: does every row have to know this? An account's status has a safe fallback, so it gets a default. Leave it out, and the row comes back active. But an account with no email makes no sense. So email is marked not null, and an insert without one is refused. Now every account has an email. But could two of them share one?

Ada signs up. Then a second account tries her email, with a new username. Duplicate key, refused. One email, one account. The primary key already keeps rows distinct. Unique guards everything else that can't repeat. It even works on pairs.

A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. So both IDs repeat... but each pair only once. Enroll student one in course ten a second time, and it bounces. Put unique on a foreign key, and each user gets at most one profile. That's one to one. That covers missing and repeated. What about values that are just wrong?

That's a check: a true or false test that every row has to pass. Price zero or more was one. Status has to be draft, active, or archived. So banana? Nope. It can compare columns, too. An event can't end before it starts, so this backwards conference never gets in.

One catch, though. A check only refuses false. Leave the price out, and the test comes back unknown... so the row slips through. That's why a required price gets three rules. Numeric for its type, a check for its range, and not null, so it's actually there.
